                      MEYER E11 INTERVENORS’ REPLY TO EXCEPTIONS

      TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

                  COMES NOW Paul & Jane Meyer Family Foundation, SM Retreat Ltd. and Leslie Meyer

      Rhea [“Meyer E11 Intervenors”], and pursuant to PUC Memo dated August 20, 2026 (Int. No.

      6442) file this Meyer E11 Intervenors’ Reply to Exceptions in the above-entitled docket:

             I.          Limited Reply - Routing

                  The Meyer E11 Intervenors are only submitting briefing on the issue of routing. Their

      Reply will focus solely on the arguments raised by intervenors advocating for Route 392 and the

      Whitis argument for Route Whitis 1-14.

            II.          Fading Advocacy for Exclusively Route 392

                  There are only five Exceptions filed in this case that advocate for Route 392. 1 Of those,

      only the one filed by the Solana Intervenors insists that Route 392 is the only choice. All the

      others, including the Brady Creek group aligned with Solana, allow for other, better options.


1
    4K Land and Cattle Co., Staten Creek Ranch, Brady Creek, Solana and John G. Yates, Jr.
                                                                                                      Page 1
 Such tacit realization that Route 392 is a poor basket to put all one’s eggs in cannot be ignored.

Even the parties arguing that there is only one viable Colorado River crossing are forced to

acknowledge that there may be better Routes using that single link than 392.

    III.         No Single River Crossing Dictates Routing Decisions

       As set out in PURA, the PUC rules and the Commission’s Order of Referral, the Proposal

for Decision correctly recommended a complete route based on an analysis of all factors as

applied to the entire length of the route. The PFD appropriately rejected the arguments to base

the routing decision for a 220+ mile long route on the sole factor of environmental impact of a

single river crossing – no matter how significant the river.

       Still, the advocates for Route 392 insist that the Colorado River crossing is the only

feature in the Study Area that differentiates the routes. The route-level analysis balancing all the

enumerated factors in PURA reveals a number of categories in which Route 392 is not merely

different, but it is truly a poor-performing outlier. This may explain why even proponents of the

U3 river crossing include other routes as options.

    IV.          Route 894 is a Better Choice than 392

           It is undeniable that Route 894 has a clear advantage over 392 in terms of cost and

habitable structure counts. As discussed in our Initial Brief, all forms of compatible right-of-way

should be examined together, and Route 894 performs better than 392 in that aspect as well.

There is no legal basis for the arguments advanced that “some ROW is more compatible than

others.” The PFD was correct in its analysis of these factors.

       As was demonstrated in our Post-Hearing Briefs, there are at least eleven routing factors

other than cost, length and habitable structures in which Routes 894 and 487 are dramatically

superior to Route 392:

     1)          Total length paralleling compatible ROW (19.5% less)

                                                                                              Page 2
      2)        Crossing potential wetlands (22.8% more)
     3)        Stream crossings (14.9% more)
     4)        Recorded cultural resource sites crossed (8 times as many)
     5)        Cultural resource sites w/in 1,000 feet (almost 3 times as many)
     6)        Length over high archeological/historical potential (28.4% more)
     7)        FAA-registered airports (50% more)
     8)        FM/microwave installations (more than twice as many)
     9)        Highway crossings (16 2/3% more)
    10)        FM/County road crossings (55.3% more)
    11)        Foreground visual zone of highways (88% more)

Route 392 is also the only one of the three that crosses any upland woodland areas, parallels

streams, or is near heliports and AM transmitters. Joint Applicants’ Exhibit 23 (Route by Miles

tab).

        When the statistical differences between Routes 894 and 392 are expressed in terms of

multipliers rather than percentage, it reveals what a true outlier Route 392 is. In terms of cultural

resources alone Route 392 bears the appearance of reversing the PURA requirements and routing

toward rather than avoiding them. All of the factors and statistical differences need to be taken

into account rather than the simplistic “cost per hab avoided” analysis offered by the Route 392

proponents.   The PFD properly considered all of the routing factors and came to correct

conclusion that Route 392 as a whole was a significantly inferior option.

   V.          Better Routes Including Link U3

        Even if the ALJs and/or Commissioners are convinced by the argument that the only

acceptable crossing of the Colorado River is Link U3 and no route containing another crossing

should be considered, as reflected by the filed Exceptions there are still better routes to select

than 392.

        The 4K Land and Cattle Company brief actually lists Route 392 third when it describes

the “Northern Corridor” routes it prefers. Int. 6478, p. 7. It advocates for Routes 410. 416 or

392. The Staten Creek Intervenors recommend Route 392 or 410, but also consider a Southern


                                                                                               Page 3
 Option like Route 296. Int. 6477 pp. 43-44. Mr. Yates prefers Routes 296, 392 or 487.

        Using the holistic, route-level analysis under PURA, both Routes 410 and 296 advocated

by the Colorado River proponents, perform significantly better than Route 392. Comparing the

three routes in a manner similar to the analysis copied above, we see that Route 392 results in not

only higher cost and length than Route 296, but 392 is also inferior on:

         1)    Habitable structures (38.7% more than 410 and 29.5% more than 296)
         2)    Total length paralleling compatible ROW (16% less than 296 and 3% less than 410)
         3)    Length paralleling transmission line ROW (12.4% less than 410)
         4)    Length crossing riparian areas (8% more than 410 and 13% more than
               296)
         5)    Crossing potential wetlands (21% more than 296)
         6)    Stream crossings (2.9% more than 410 and 8% more than 296)
         7)    Recorded cultural resource sites crossed (4 times as many as 296)
         8)    Cultural resource sites w/in 1,000 feet (over 2.6 times as many as 296)
         9)    Length over high archeological/historical potential (1% more than 410 and 22.55%
               more than 296)
        10)    FAA-registered airports (28.6% more than 296)
        11)    FM/microwave installations (37.5% more than 410 and 22.2% more than 296)
        12)    FM/County road crossings (19.7% more than 296)
        13)    Foreground visual zone of highways (3.3% more than 410 and 62.5% more
               than 296

        As can be seen, the difference in habitable structures impacted is dramatically higher for

392 than either Route 410 or 296.      Routes 410 and 296 are also superior to 392 in at least

thirteen other PURA factors based on the statistical data in the record. Even if the analysis is

narrowed severely to accept the assumption that the only viable crossing of the Colorado River is

Link U3, the proper route choice is Route 410, not 392.

  VI.          Whitis 1-14 is Even Worse

        Whitis Land Investments is the only intervenor to advocate for Route Whitis 1-14. It was

not a Focus Route in the PFD, nor was it identified as a potential Route of Interest by the Joint

applicants. Reviewing the data reveals why. It is truly a route only its author could love.

        Almost unbelievably, Whitis 1-4 impacts more habitable structures than even Route 392.


                                                                                              Page 4
 It has a higher habitable structure count than any of the Focus Routes or potential Routes of

Interest. It underperforms under a number of other factors. There is nothing in prior PUC CCN

cases that would suggest that intentionally choosing a route with the most habitable structures for

incremental cost savings would be a rational decision.

  VII.          Conclusion

         The PFD appropriately applied the required holistic review of the routing factors set forth

in PURA and the PUC rules to the entirety of the evidentiary record so painstakingly developed.

The result was its alternative selection of Route 894. The proponents for Route 392 begin and

end their analysis with the Colorado River crossing. Even if the ALJs are somehow persuaded

that the Colorado River crossing is the only decision that matters in this case, and that the only

acceptable crossing of the Colorado River is Link U3, Route 410 is a superior route to 392 after

reviewing the PURA factors and the record. Route 296 outperforms both in a number of

important factors. The ask that After due consideration of the evidentiary record and all the

routing factors, the Meyer E11 Intervenors see no justification for changing the alternative

routing recommendation in the Proposal for Decision.
